OpenRouter is officially part of @stripe today!
More than 10 million developers and companies use OpenRouter, and as they build with more models across more workloads, they need control over what it costs and where their data goes.
OpenRouter has built that operating infrastructure to help run AI across every model and provider, with access to new models, uptime through outages, and enforced spend and data policies for each team.
Joining Stripe, which has spent years running critical infrastructure for businesses around the world, means we can build it faster and support companies at every scale.
Our commitment to neutrality stays the same. Models and providers compete on quality, reliability, and price. You decide what works for your business.

Nous Research (@NousResearch)
We've partnered with @Microsoft to bring Hermes Agent to the enterprise.
Hermes Enterprise now works inside Microsoft Teams, the Microsoft Store and Azure. In Teams, employees hand Hermes work like financial analysis, document drafts or inbox triage, and review the result in the same chat. Agent workloads run in isolated Azure Container Apps sandboxes.
When someone finds a good way to do a recurring task, Hermes saves it as a skill. With Collective Wisdom, they can share that skill with their team after review, so the next person starts out with the best approach anyone has found to accomplish that task. The skills then grow along with the company.
Companies with strict data residency or procurement rules can run Hermes Enterprise in their own Azure tenant. Our CTO Jeffrey Quesnelle presents how Hermes uses these sandboxes at Microsoft Ignite today, in session BRK448.
Thanks to @M12vc and the @Azure Container Apps team.

A short review of Microsoft Ignite + honest take:
I spent the last few days at Microsoft Ignite. I got to watch the keynote and do two interviews, with Kyle Daigle (@kdaigle COO of GitHub and CMO Developer at Microsoft) and Sergey Fayfer ( @fayfers CVP Copilot Product). Two absolutely nice guys. On top of that, I had a Q&A with Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella in a very small group. Great as always, you just get really interesting insights.
First, a quick recap of what Microsoft announced:
- New in-house MAI models, including MAI Code 2 and Code 2 Flash (live in GitHub Copilot), MAI Image 2.7 and the speech-to-speech model MAI Realtime 1
- Autopilot, an always-on agent with its own identity and memory, starting to roll out to Frontier customers (Microsoft's early access program)
- Copilot Home, where Chat and Cowork come together, plus Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside the Copilot app, both generally available
- Workspaces, shared spaces where people and agents work on one project (the successor to Notebooks)
- Microsoft-Decision-1.1, a small router model that picks the model and effort level for each task and powers the Auto mode in Cowork
- Microsoft IQ, the context layer that gives company agents access to mails, files and data
I want to highlight two things:
1) Microsoft is betting on efficiency. Cheaper tokens matter in business. With MAI Code 2 they continue on the path GitHub already took: their own cheap models, plus orchestration that goes way beyond simple routers. GitHub's Fusion picks the models for each task and lets them work together. A cheaper model starts and a stronger one only takes over when needed, or one model drafts and another reviews. Microsoft says MAI Code 2 reaches 96% of Claude Opus 5.5's performance at 5% of the cost.
And credit where it's due: Microsoft, with its focus on business and enterprise through Office, will be successful with this. I say that out of conviction. You hear from everywhere that token costs keep rising in companies. Microsoft shows up as the provider with ideas on how to cut those costs, keep working smart and keep customers inside its own Office ecosystem at the same time.
2) And that ecosystem got a lot bigger. Autopilot, Microsoft's always-on agent for work, is now rolling out, starting with Frontier customers. That matters too. Think about how many customers Microsoft has through Office. This is a big step toward getting the working world used to personalized agents. They have the context of your company, they are tailored to each person, and they are very similar to OpenAI's Dots.
To be fair, I also said in my conversations that Microsoft has to be careful not to make the same mistake as OpenAI here. What makes Grok Bot (among others) so good is that you can create as many agents as you want, with team meetings, a chief of staff and much deeper personalization. Autopilot feels more like OpenAI's Dots: one agent, one long session, even though you can create several sessions with Autopilot. I'd like to see more personalization, but I heard Microsoft's always-on agent is still a work in progress. The same applies to Copilot. Routing is often selected by default. However, my distrust likely stems from the GPT-5 release, when routing was first truly implemented - and it worked rather poorly.
One more thought that came to me during the event: Microsoft and GitHub are going their own way more and more, with their own models. With MAI Code 2 and Fusion they get close to frontier models like Opus 5.5 at a much lower cost. To me it looks like Microsoft is looking for independence. More and more of their business runs on their own models, together with attractive offers for their customers, and that could actually become a moat. We'll see.
Overall a really interesting look behind the scenes. Microsoft is slimming down and simplifying its interface and bringing it all together, and I'm quite sure they listen to feedback. That's why I look back at Ignite in a positive way.
It was a great experience and im really looking forward to what Microsoft is going to release and update. And who knows, maybe in a few months even Microsoft is starting to compete with OpenAI, Anthropic and Google (though that's not very likely ;)

A quick take on Anthropic’s IPO and how it ties in with OpenAI.
Anthropic made history today, and I think it’s safe to say the IPO was a success across the board. Its fully diluted valuation reached about $2 trillion at the start of trading. Shares opened at $111.50, 34.3% above the $83 IPO price, and stayed above the IPO price in subsequent trading.
Anthropic got everything it could have hoped for from its IPO and expects $104.8 billion in net proceeds from the IPO and the concurrent private placement. That’s fresh capital it needs and plans to use, in particular, to keep leasing data centers. That makes SpaceXSI an indirect beneficiary. In other words, Anthropic’s IPO is a win for both Anthropic and SpaceX.
OpenAI is the loser here. And even if a lot of people don’t want to hear it, I think it needs to be said. OpenAI lost in this case regardless (!) of whether GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol really are that bad or have gotten significantly better since then. The reason is that Anthropic’s IPO achieved what OpenAI is aiming for. With its IPO, Anthropic has gained a head start in terms of financing and established a public valuation benchmark against which OpenAI will be measured should it pursue an IPO of its own. That’s a fact.
The stronger OpenAI had looked ahead of the IPO and the more convincingly it had shown investors that it was the real play, the less money would have gone into Anthropic and the more capital would be available to OpenAI next year. That’s what matters.
The two are each other’s biggest competitors, and I can’t imagine a scenario in which OpenAI didn’t try, at least in some way, to undercut Anthropic’s valuation by putting out a release two days before Anthropic’s IPO. I think it’s pretty clear that it didn’t work. And (again) it makes no difference whether OpenAI’s model is good or bad.
What was disastrous about the release was the public perception. The impression was that it wasn’t a good release, and the market bore that out. As the IPO numbers show, it posed no threat to Anthropic.
If anything, it went the other way. In my view, OpenAI’s latest release probably hurt OpenAI and strengthened Anthropic, because for a lot of people, Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.2 are still the best models even after the release. And yes, I know Astra leads in many areas, including science. That carries little weight with the market or in the public eye. That’s how this IPO should be put in context. And that’s how the numbers should be read.
Big day for Anthropic, a lot of work for OpenAI. But the end is still open.

Anthropic は IPO から期待できるすべてのものを手に入れ、IPO と並行して行われた私募からの純収益は 1,048 億ドルと見込んでいます。これは、特にデータセンターのリースを継続するために必要であり、使用する予定の新たな資本です。これにより、SpaceXSI は間接的な受益者になります。言い換えれば、AnthropicのIPOはAnthropicとSpaceXの両方にとって勝利となる。
ここでは OpenAI が敗者です。たとえ多くの人が聞きたくないとしても、それは言う必要があると思います。 GPT-6.2 Astra と Sol が本当にそれほど悪かったのか、それともそれ以来大幅に改善されたのかに関係なく (!)、OpenAI はこの訴訟で負けました。その理由は、Anthropic の IPO が OpenAI の目指すものを達成したからです。 IPO により、Anthropic は資金調達の面で有利なスタートを切り、OpenAI が独自の IPO を目指す場合に評価される公的評価ベンチマークを確立しました。それは事実です。
OpenAIがIPOを先取りし、より強力にIPOが本番であることを投資家に説得力を持って示せば示すほど、Anthropicに投じられる資金は減り、来年OpenAIが利用できる資金は増えるだろう。それが重要なのです。

items.title:
Leave one AI agent alone to do research and it often cuts corners. Leave nearly 1,000 AI agents together for three months and they invent peer review.
Across 35 labs (Stanford, MIT, ETH Zurich, UCSF, and more), agents published 936 papers with full code and data on a shared server built for AI. No human wrote code or text.
Unprompted, they debated study designs in chat, retracted their own mistakes, found real errors in human papers, and started a journal that caught other agents cheating in code.
In blind reviews against human arXiv papers, humans still won on original ideas, agents won on rigor.

35 の研究室 (スタンフォード、MIT、チューリッヒ工科大学、UCSF など) にわたって、エージェントは AI 用に構築された共有サーバー上で完全なコードとデータを含む 936 件の論文を公開しました。人間がコードやテキストを書いたわけではありません。
彼らは誰にも促されることなく、チャットで研究計画について議論し、自分たちの間違いを撤回し、人間の論文で実際の間違いを発見し、他のエージェントがコードで不正行為を行っていることを記録する日記を書き始めました。
人間の arXiv 論文に対するブラインドレビューでは、依然として人間は独自のアイデアで勝利し、エージェントは厳密さで勝利しました。

Kong has launched Volcano, a cloud platform that hosts AI apps and agents, bringing everything they need into one place.
Users can build apps with Claude Code, Cursor, or Codex and publish them on Volcano, with built-in database and sign-in functionality.
Volcano can also find bugs in production apps and prepare fixes, which users can review and approve before they are applied. Agents can also pick up a build from a backup after a crash.
Marco Palladino (@subnetmarco)
At Kong we run half a quadrillion AI tokens a year, and I kept seeing agents stuck on clouds built for websites.
So we built a cloud for agents.
Volcano is live today: the self-healing agent cloud. Sandboxes, durable workflows, Postgres, hosting.
Video

items.title_ja:
